en.name: Byblos
en.note: Lived in for roughly seven thousand years, and still a working fishing harbour.
en.standfirst: Seven thousand years of people, stacked. The crusader keep sits on Roman, on Phoenician, on Bronze Age, and the harbour below it still works.
en.body: Byblos is the argument for staying put. Every civilisation that arrived built on what the last one left rather than clearing it, so the site reads as a section drawing rather than a ruin. You can stand at one corner and see four thousand years of wall in a single glance. The alphabet that became Greek and then Latin shipped out of the harbour at the bottom of the hill, which is now about the size of a car park and full of fishing boats.

en.label: Crusader keep
en.body: Twelfth century, built from Roman columns laid on their sides as bracing.

en.label: The harbour
en.body: Still working. Boats leave from the north wall most mornings.

en.label: Royal necropolis
en.body: Nine shaft tombs. The Ahiram sarcophagus carried the earliest long alphabetic text.

en.label: Getting there
en.value: 40 km north of Beirut · 45 min by road

en.label: Best season
en.value: April–June, September–November

en.label: Entry
en.value: Ticketed site; the old town and harbour are free

en.name: Baalbek
en.note: The Temple of Jupiter sits on three foundation blocks of about eight hundred tonnes each.
en.standfirst: The largest Roman temple ever built, standing on three foundation stones that nobody has satisfactorily explained moving.
en.body: The Temple of Jupiter had fifty-four columns. Six are still standing, and they are twenty-two metres tall. Underneath them the podium contains the trilithon: three limestone blocks of roughly eight hundred tonnes each. A fourth, larger still, remains in the quarry eight hundred metres to the south, half-cut and abandoned. Whatever method moved the first three was clearly at its limit. The site sits in the Bekaa at a thousand metres, which is why the light here is harder and clearer than on the coast.

en.label: The trilithon
en.body: Three blocks, roughly 800 tonnes each, in the western podium wall.

en.label: Six columns
en.body: All that stands of fifty-four. Twenty-two metres to the capital.

en.label: Temple of Bacchus
en.body: Better preserved than anything in Rome, and larger than the Parthenon.

en.label: Getting there
en.value: 85 km east of Beirut · 2 hr over the Dahr el-Baidar pass

en.label: Best season
en.value: May–October. The pass can close in winter

en.label: Entry
en.value: Ticketed. The quarry megalith is outside the fence and free

en.name: Jeita Grotto
en.note: Nine kilometres of surveyed limestone galleries on two levels, one of them navigated by boat.
en.standfirst: Nine kilometres of surveyed limestone gallery on two levels. You walk the upper one and take a boat through the lower.
en.body: The Nahr al-Kalb cut these galleries out of the limestone over a few million years and is still doing it. The upper cavern holds one of the largest known stalactites at about eight metres, and the acoustics are good enough that concerts have been held inside. The lower level is a river, navigated by flat-bottomed boat for a few hundred metres before the guides turn you around. Photography is not allowed inside, which is unusual now and worth knowing before you carry a camera up.

en.label: Upper gallery
en.body: Walkable. The 8 m stalactite is roughly a third of the way in.

en.label: Boat turnaround
en.body: The lower river is navigable in winter only when the water is low enough.

en.label: Cable car
en.body: Links the entrance to the upper cavern. Worth taking up, walking down.

en.label: Getting there
en.value: 18 km north of Beirut · 30 min

en.label: Best season
en.value: Year round. The lower grotto closes when the river is high

en.label: Hours
en.value: 09:00 – 18:00, closed Mondays out of season

en.label: Note
en.value: No cameras inside. Lockers at the entrance

en.name: The Cedars of God
en.note: A surviving grove at roughly two thousand metres, with trees over a thousand years old.
en.standfirst: Horsh Arz el-Rab. The Forest of the Cedars of God. A few hundred trunks at two thousand metres, some of them a thousand years old.
en.body: This is the tree on the flag, and there is not much of it left. Fences went up in the nineteenth century because goats were eating every seedling before it could root, and the grove has been managed ever since. Snow closes the road above Bsharri for part of most winters. The trees have handled roughly forty of those winters per human lifetime. Stand under the oldest ones and the scale is not height, it is girth: some of the trunks take four people to reach around.

en.label: The old grove
en.body: A few hundred trees. The oldest are estimated above a thousand years.

en.label: Replanting
en.body: Seedlings behind the fence line, planted from the 1990s onward.

en.label: Snowline
en.body: The road from Bsharri closes here in heavy winters.

en.label: Getting there
en.value: 120 km from Beirut · 2 hr 30 via Bsharri

en.label: Best season
en.value: June–October for walking, January–March for snow

en.label: Altitude
en.value: ~2,000 m. Bring a layer even in summer

en.label: Entry
en.value: Small fee at the grove gate

en.name: Qadisha Valley
en.note: Monks cut hermitages into the cliff faces here and stayed for centuries.
en.standfirst: A gorge with monasteries cut into its walls. People moved in to be left alone and stayed for a thousand years.
en.body: Qadisha means holy, and the valley earned it by being difficult to reach. Monks and hermits cut cells and chapels directly into the cliff faces, some of them only reachable by a path that is still a scramble. The valley floor is walkable end to end in a long day, and the drop from the rim at Bsharri to the river is close to a kilometre. It is on the UNESCO list jointly with the cedar grove above it, which is the correct way to list them. One is the reason the other survived.

en.label: Deir Qannoubine
en.body: Cut into the rock face. Patriarchal seat for roughly five centuries.

en.label: Valley floor
en.body: The Qadisha river. Walkable end to end in a long day.

en.label: Bsharri rim
en.body: Roughly a kilometre above the river. The cedar grove is behind it.

en.label: Getting there
en.value: 110 km from Beirut · 2 hr 15

en.label: Best season
en.value: April–November. The paths ice over in winter

en.label: Walking
en.value: Rim to floor and back is a full day. Guides available in Bsharri

en.label: Entry
en.value: Free. Individual monasteries have their own hours

en.name: Tyre
en.note: The Roman hippodrome on the edge of town held tens of thousands for chariot racing.
en.standfirst: Alexander built a causeway to take this island. The sand never left, and Tyre has been a peninsula ever since.
en.body: Tyre was an island city and it was, for a long time, unconquerable. Alexander solved that in 332 BC by building a mole out to it from the mainland, and the mole silted up, permanently joining the two. The Roman hippodrome on the landward side held tens of thousands for chariot racing and is one of the largest ever found. The city below is still a working fishing port with a good beach at the end of it, which is a more useful combination than most archaeological sites manage.

en.label: Hippodrome
en.body: Roman, one of the largest known. The turning posts are still in place.

en.label: The causeway
en.body: Alexander's mole, now permanently silted into an isthmus.

en.label: Fishing harbour
en.body: Still working. The beach runs south from it.

en.label: Getting there
en.value: 83 km south of Beirut · 1 hr 30

en.label: Best season
en.value: May–October for the beach; year round for the site

en.label: Entry
en.value: Two ticketed sites. Al-Bass and the marine city

en.name: Beirut
en.note: Rebuilt after each of the seven times it was destroyed, which is how the city argues with itself.
en.standfirst: Destroyed seven times and rebuilt seven times, which is why the city argues with itself in every direction at once.
en.body: Beirut does not resolve. A Roman bath sits under an office block, a French Mandate façade stands beside raw concrete, and the Corniche runs five kilometres along the sea past fishermen, cyclists, families, and at least one man selling roasted corn. The sea stacks at Raouche are a hundred metres offshore and half the city walks past them every evening and still stops to look. Come for the food and stay for the fact that nobody here agrees on what the city is.

en.label: The Corniche
en.body: Five kilometres of seafront promenade. Best at dusk.

en.label: Raouche
en.body: Two limestone stacks a hundred metres offshore.

en.label: Downtown
en.body: Roman baths, Ottoman souk lines, Mandate façades, all within a few streets.

en.label: Getting there
en.value: Beirut–Rafic Hariri airport is 9 km from downtown

en.label: Best season
en.value: April–June, September–November

en.label: Getting around
en.value: Taxis and service (shared) taxis. Walkable along the coast

en.label: Note
en.value: Cash economy in most places. Bring US dollars

en.name: Batroun
en.note: A Phoenician sea wall still takes the swell off the old harbour.
en.standfirst: A Phoenician sea wall still takes the swell off the old harbour, and the town behind it has become the coast’s best evening.
en.body: The wall is the thing: a natural sandstone ridge that the Phoenicians extended and squared off, and it has been breaking the Mediterranean for the town for something like three thousand years. Batroun is small, walkable, and has quietly become where people from Beirut go for a weekend. Old stone streets, a lot of good seafood, and lemonade that the town is genuinely known for. The vineyards start about twenty minutes inland.

en.label: The Phoenician wall
en.body: Natural ridge, squared and extended. Still doing its job.

en.label: Old town
en.body: Sandstone streets behind the harbour, walkable end to end.

en.label: Vineyards
en.body: Twenty minutes inland, on the limestone slopes.

en.label: Getting there
en.value: 54 km north of Beirut · 1 hr

en.label: Best season
en.value: May–October

en.label: Worth ordering
en.value: Lemonade, and whatever came in that morning

en.label: Entry
en.value: Free. It is a town, not a site
